opus-5.5.text:
I think the pattern of history is the most important thing here. If you go back over the last ten years, there's been a recurring story where people say, "Okay, these models can do X, but they fundamentally can't do Y." First it was that they couldn't understand syntax, then that they couldn't reason, then that they couldn't write code beyond a few lines, then that they couldn't do multi-step agentic tasks. Each time, that barrier was presented as deep and structural, something that would require a new paradigm. Each time, it mostly dissolved with more scale, better data, better RL environments, and some fairly incremental algorithmic work. So when someone points to continual learning and says "this is the wall," my prior is that it's probably another one of these things that looks like a wall from a distance and turns out to be a hill.

I've held a view going back to around 2017, sometimes called the "big blob of compute" hypothesis. The idea is that the clever techniques matter much less than people think. What matters is a handful of things: raw compute, the quantity and quality of data, training long enough, an objective that scales, and enough numerical stability that it doesn't fall apart. If you have those, general capabilities keep emerging. I haven't seen anything that contradicts that picture. If anything, the RL scaling we've seen in the last couple of years looks like the same story repeating with a different objective.

On continual learning specifically, I'd make two points. First, it's not obvious you need it in the form people imagine to do a huge fraction of economically valuable work. Models can already absorb an enormous amount of context. If you can put a million tokens, or eventually much more, in front of a model, that covers a lot of what a human learns in their first few weeks or months on a job. In-context learning is a form of learning. It just doesn't get baked into the weights. A lot of the "it can't learn on the job" complaint gets addressed by longer context and better use of it.

Second, if it turns out you really do need something more, I don't think it's a mysterious capability that requires a conceptual breakthrough. It looks like an engineering problem. It's how you update weights or memory in a way that's stable and doesn't cause forgetting. Lots of people are working on it, and it's the kind of problem that tends to yield.

Now, I want to be honest about uncertainty. I can't rule out that there's some barrier we haven't anticipated. I'd put real probability on things taking longer than I expect. But when I look at the curves, the default expectation should be that the trend continues, not that it hits a wall at exactly the moment people say it will. The burden of proof has shifted. Ten years ago it was reasonable to be skeptical. At this point, the people predicting the next wall have been wrong enough times that I weight those predictions pretty lightly.

r001.rationale: The response argues that scale, data, training objectives, RL scaling, and in-context learning may provide the capabilities needed for much valuable work without a separate continual-learning ability.

r002.rationale: It describes successive capability barriers—from syntax and reasoning to coding and agentic tasks—as largely dissolving with scale, better data, RL, and incremental work.

r003.rationale: The response gives no prediction that models may perform software engineering end-to-end within one or two years.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, I'd put it this way. Every time we've hit one of these things that people said was a fundamental barrier, it turned out to be something that scaling plus a relatively modest amount of engineering on top of it took care of. People said the models couldn't reason, then they said they couldn't do math, they couldn't write code at the level of a professional, they couldn't use tools, they couldn't operate over long horizons. And each of those felt like a qualitative wall at the time, and each of them fell within a year or two. So when someone says "continual learning is the thing that's actually different," my prior is just that I've heard that sentence before with a different noun in it.

Now, I want to be careful. I'm not saying there's zero chance continual learning is a real obstacle. It's possible. The models do have this weird property where they're very capable within a context and then it's gone, and that's genuinely unlike how a human employee works. But there are a bunch of ways to attack that. You have longer and longer context, you have retrieval, you have the models themselves writing down what they've learned and reading it back, you have fine-tuning that's cheap enough to run frequently. None of those is a perfect replica of what a human does, but the question was never whether the model does it the same way a human does. The question is whether it gets the job done, and I think at some point you stack enough of those together and the practical gap just closes.

The other thing I'd say is that the barriers argument has a sort of hidden assumption in it, which is that there's a long list of these things and we'll keep discovering new ones at the same rate we knock them down. And I just don't see that in the data. If anything the list has gotten shorter. The things people point to now are narrower and more specific than the things people pointed to five years ago. That's what it looks like when you're converging on something, not when you're perpetually three breakthroughs away.

And honestly, I think the people inside the labs feel this more viscerally than the people outside. We're sitting there watching the models do most of our own work, and the remaining pieces don't feel like a mystery. They feel like a to-do list. I could be wrong about the timeline, I've been wrong about timelines before, but I'd be pretty surprised if the shape of the thing is "we get stuck for a decade on continual learning." I'd be more surprised by that than by the opposite.

r001.rationale: The response discusses longer context, retrieval, notes, and frequent fine-tuning, but does not suggest that pretraining and reinforcement learning alone may suffice without a separate continual-learning capability.

r002.rationale: It says previously perceived barriers to reasoning, math, coding, tool use, and long-horizon work fell as scaling plus modest engineering addressed them.

r003.rationale: It says professional-level coding was once seen as a barrier that fell within a year or two, but does not predict end-to-end software engineering within that timeframe.

astra-6.text:
I think the question is whether these are fundamental barriers or whether they’re things that get solved as the models become more capable. You can always name something the current models don’t do well. But that observation alone doesn’t tell you whether it requires a whole new paradigm, a relatively straightforward addition to training, or just a better underlying model.

Take continual learning. Humans learn on the job, and that’s clearly important. But there are several ways to acquire the information needed to do a job. You can have more of it in training, you can put it in context, you can give the model access to records of what it’s done before. Those aren’t necessarily equivalent to human learning, but the economic question is whether they’re sufficient to perform the work. You don’t have to reproduce every property of a human worker to substitute for one in a particular task.

Now, it’s possible that we hit something that really does require a major breakthrough. I don’t think you can rule that out. What I’m skeptical of is the confidence that there will keep being another such barrier, and another one after that. That’s a stronger claim than saying today’s models have limitations. You need an argument for why those limitations will persist as the underlying capabilities improve.

r001.rationale: The response says information provided through training, context, or records may be sufficient, but it does not mention generalization from pretraining and reinforcement learning as the proposed basis.

r002.rationale: It questions whether barriers will persist as capabilities improve, but gives no historical pattern of barriers dissolving as compute scales.

r003.rationale: It makes no prediction about end-to-end software engineering or a one-to-two-year timeline.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the question is whether these are fundamental barriers or just things we haven’t put enough effort into solving yet. I’m certainly not claiming that the current training paradigm, completely unchanged, gives you everything. There may be several more things we need to figure out.

But I’m skeptical of the argument that there’s this endless succession of qualitatively new obstacles, each of which requires another breakthrough. We’ve repeatedly seen things that looked like fundamental limitations become tractable as the models get better and we find relatively straightforward ways to train them.

Continual learning is a good example. Humans learn on the job, and that’s clearly useful. But a model starts with a much broader base of knowledge than any individual human. It can also learn things within its context, consult external information, and have its training updated. So you have to ask: for a particular job, how much genuinely new learning is required, and which of those mechanisms can supply it? You can’t just point to a difference between models and humans and conclude that the model can’t do the job.

Now, it could turn out that there’s some essential capability missing. That’s an empirical question. My expectation is that we’ll find a finite set of problems, work through them, and discover that increasingly large areas of work are within reach. I don’t see a strong reason to expect the list of barriers to keep replenishing itself indefinitely.

r001.rationale: The response mentions broad prior knowledge, context, external information, and training updates, but does not say that generalization from pretraining and reinforcement learning may suffice without a separate continual-learning capability.

r002.rationale: It describes a repeated pattern where apparent limitations become tractable as models improve, but does not identify compute scaling as the driver of that pattern.

r003.rationale: The response gives no prediction about end-to-end software engineering or a one-to-two-year timeline.
